doc.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010

title: Partnership with Eric Alexander and ten pianists at Bradley's
summary: He praises Eric Alexander's fitness and talent, and recalls a Bradley's night when ten pianists came to hear him.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Yeah. And you seem to have found a good partner working relationship with Eric Alexander.

I can’t say enough about him. He’s so phenomenal and he gets better and he’s so smart. Expert skier. He ran the Chicago marathon a few years ago just to do it, and out of 27,000 he finished in the top 600 and the winning time was 2 hours and 8 minutes and Eric’s finishing time was 2 hours and 50 minutes. Do you believe that? Long distance runner. When we go to Japan, he’ll run two hours before the gig. You know? So I have tremendous respect for him because first of all you’ve got to be in some kind of physical shape to play this music. Now if you’re just sitting up there, talking about cocktail china, that’s okay, well you just play. But if you’re talking about hard core swinging hard stamina, and as a piano player I’ve got to play three to four to five choruses behind these players, I’ve got to be physically in shape. You know what I’m saying. So I feel very blessed that the Creator bestowed this little bit of talent on me so since I got it, I just try to pursue it more and get better. Because every day you learn something. It’s something you put in your sack of surprises, musically speaking, or whatever. Because you need your bag of tricks because when some of the guys come around, they’re coming to hear some of them, the piano players. I remember one time I played at a place called Bradley’s. It might have been a one night gig. Ten piano players came. Sir Roland Hanna, Jackie Byard now that’s another unsung hero he was, Jackie Byard man, oh, what a tremendous musician. But he never got his total recognition. George Coleman never got his total recognition that he deserved. And the most underrated, unappreciated musician of all time is Phineas Newborn Junior. And to this day I don’t understand that. Maybe it’s jealousy. It’s like how dare you to be that good? Here’s a man that could put his right hand in his pocket and play complete competition with his right hand. There’s a record called “Will of the Piano.” I bought it up here with me, that every piano player should have. So Hank Jones once said, “I’m trying to figure out what it is about Phineas.
